title: Act III, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: Caesar brushes aside the soothsayer ('the ides of March are come') and refuses to read Artemidorus's letter first. Trebonius draws Antony away. Metellus Cimber pleads for his banished brother; Caesar refuses, calling himself 'constant as the northern star.' Casca strikes first; the others stab; Brutus strikes last ('Et tu, Brute? Then fall, Caesar!'). The conspirators bathe their hands in Caesar's blood and cry liberty. Antony sends a servant, then comes himself, shakes their bloody hands and asks to speak at the funeral. Brutus agrees over Cassius's objection, on condition that Antony speaks after him and does not blame them. Alone, Antony prophesies civil war ('Cry Havoc, and let slip the dogs of war'). News comes that Octavius is near Rome.

context.history: The real assassination took place on 15 March 44 BC in the Theatre of Pompey, where the Senate was meeting; Shakespeare sets it at the Capitol. The words 'Et tu, Brute?' come from earlier English tradition, not Plutarch.

significance: The climax comes at the midpoint of the play. Brutus's second mistake (letting Antony speak) turns the play from a story of conspiracy into one of revenge.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act III, Scene I,” how does Shakespeare show the assassination? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the conflict you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act III, Scene I, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of the assassination? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the conflict in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act III, Scene I develops the idea of the assassination. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of conflict and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act III, Scene I (where it begins, turns and ends) and its conflict shape the reader's understanding of the assassination. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act III, Scene I suggests about the assassination. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's conflict and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses conflict in Act III, Scene I to complicate the reader's understanding of the assassination. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act III, Scene I within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the assassination responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act III, Scene I alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the assassination follows or bends those conventions, using the conflict as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act III, Scene I and its treatment of the assassination. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's conflict and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act III, Scene I as evidence for a larger claim about the assassination in Julius Caesar. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act III, Scene I as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the assassination. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Julius Caesar.

satQuestions.passage:
I must prevent thee, Cimber.
These couchings and these lowly courtesies
Might fire the blood of ordinary men,
And turn pre-ordinance and first decree
Into the law of children. Be not fond,
To think that Caesar bears such rebel blood
That will be thaw’d from the true quality
With that which melteth fools; I mean, sweet words,
Low-crooked court’sies and base spaniel-fawning.
Thy brother by decree is banished:
If thou dost bend and pray and fawn for him,
I spurn thee like a cur out of my way.
Know, Caesar doth not wrong, nor without cause
Will he be satisfied.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why might a story place its most famous event in the middle rather than at the end? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: This scene shows a political killing on stage.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script:
Today's words are purpled, enfranchisement, doomsday, pulpits, abridged. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “I do beseech ye, if you bear me hard,
Now, whilst your purpled hands do reek and smoke,
Fulfil your pleasure.” In this sentence it means: stained red with blood. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Julius Caesar would have known. The real assassination took place on 15 March 44 BC in the Theatre of Pompey, where the Senate was meeting; Shakespeare sets it at the Capitol. The words 'Et tu, Brute?' come from earlier English tradition, not Plutarch. Why does this scene matter? The climax comes at the midpoint of the play. Brutus's second mistake (letting Antony speak) turns the play from a story of conspiracy into one of revenge. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for conflict.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “I must prevent thee, Cimber.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the assassination? I circle “fawning”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find conflict, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for conflict.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of conflict. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this scene connect to power, ambition and tyranny? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Scene quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the scene quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this scene suggests about the assassination, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how conflict shapes the assassination. Tonight, read the next scene and add two words to your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
